Grinders
grīn´dẽrz
n. pl. (the grinding teeth; the molars)
From grind, Saxon grindan. The Preacher uses the word of the teeth, in the allegory of old age that closes Ecclesiastes — a house whose servants are failing one by one.

Biblical Definition

Ecclesiastes closes with a portrait of a body described as a great house falling into disrepair: “In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened” (Ecclesiastes 12:3). The keepers that tremble are the hands, the strong men that bow are the legs, the grinders are the teeth, and the darkened windows are the eyes. The Preacher is not being coy; he is being merciful, giving a young man a picture he can carry before he needs it. The charge that governs the whole passage stands at its head: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them” (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The decline ends where every man's does: “Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets” (Ecclesiastes 12:5). And then the verdict that sets the whole book upright: “Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7). Few teeth are a small thing. They are also a notice.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines grinder as one that grinds; and the grinders, the double teeth which serve to grind the food.

expand to see more

GRINDER, n. One that grinds, or makes smooth by grinding; a grinding tooth; a double tooth; a molar.

GRIND, v.t. [Sax. grindan.] To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction.

TOOTH, n. A bony substance growing out of the jaws, and serving as the instrument of mastication.

DECAY, v.i. To pass gradually from a sound, prosperous or perfect state, to a less perfect state; to fail.

ALLEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it.

Ecclesiastes 12:3 — "In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened,"

Ecclesiastes 12:1 — "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;"

Modern Corruption

Ageing is reframed as a problem to be managed or defeated, and Ecclesiastes 12 is read as pessimism rather than as the kindest chapter in the book.

expand to see more

A culture that markets the reversal of age cannot read Ecclesiastes 12 without flinching, and so it does not read it. The chapter is filed under the Preacher's gloom and the reader moves on. But the passage is not lamenting decline; it is timing an appeal. Every image — the trembling hands, the bowed legs, the few grinders, the darkened windows — exists to give urgency to the imperative in verse 1, which is to remember the Creator while there is still strength to remember Him with. The honesty about the body is the mercy in the text, not the sorrow in it.

The second misreading is churchly sentimentality about the elderly, which honours age in the abstract while avoiding what Ecclesiastes says about it plainly: desire fails, fears come, and man goes to his long home. Scripture never pretends otherwise, and it never leaves the picture there. Dust returns to the earth and the spirit returns unto God who gave it — which means the decay of the house is not the end of the tenant, and that the One to be remembered in youth is the One to be met at the last. The doctrine is resurrection, and it is the only ground on which a man can look at his own failing grinders without despair.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tochanah (H2913), the grinding teeth; shamar (H8104), to keep or watch; ruach (H7307), spirit or breath; bore (H1254), Creator.

expand to see more

Hebrew tochanoth (H2913) — the grinders, the grinding teeth of Ecclesiastes 12:3.

Hebrew shomerim (H8104) — the keepers of the house, the hands that tremble.

Hebrew bore (H1254) — Creator; remember now thy Creator, Ecclesiastes 12:1.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, breath; the spirit that returns unto God.

Hebrew aphar (H6083) — dust; that to which the body returns.

Usage

"“The grinders cease because they are few” — the teeth in the Preacher's allegory."

"“Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth” — the charge the picture serves."

"“The spirit shall return unto God who gave it” — the end of the matter."
